title: Your First Workflow
subtitle: Build a real CI workflow — checkout, setup, install, test, lint, and build in one file

content.text: A complete CI workflow — step by step

content.code:
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

# Cancel in-progress runs on new push (saves CI minutes)
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  ci:
    name: Test, Lint & Build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Step 1: Get the code
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Step 2: Install Node.js with npm caching
      - name: Setup Node.js 20
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'   # automatically caches ~/.npm between runs

      # Step 3: Install dependencies (ci is faster + reproducible from lock file)
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Step 4: TypeScript type check
      - name: Type check
        run: npx tsc --noEmit

      # Step 5: ESLint
      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      # Step 6: Unit tests with coverage
      - name: Test
        run: npm test -- --coverage

      # Step 7: Upload coverage report as artifact (viewable in GitHub UI)
      - name: Upload coverage
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-report
          path: coverage/
          retention-days: 7

      # Step 8: Build (only if all above pass)
      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

      # Step 9: Upload build output as artifact
      - name: Upload build
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/
          retention-days: 1   # short — used by next deploy job

content.filename: Manual cache control (when auto-cache isn't enough)
content.code:
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4

  # actions/cache saves and restores a directory between runs
  # Cache key: if package-lock.json changes, the cache is invalidated
  - name: Cache node_modules
    uses: actions/cache@v4
    with:
      path: ~/.npm
      key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
      restore-keys: |
        ${{ runner.os }}-node-

  # With Turbo (monorepo):
  - name: Cache Turborepo
    uses: actions/cache@v4
    with:
      path: .turbo
      key: ${{ runner.os }}-turbo-${{ github.sha }}
      restore-keys: |
        ${{ runner.os }}-turbo-

  - run: npm ci
  - run: npm run build   # turbo uses .turbo cache — only rebuilds what changed

content.text: Working with step outputs and environment

content.code:
steps:
  # Set an environment variable for all subsequent steps
  - name: Set build vars
    run: |
      echo "BUILD_DATE=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%d)" >> $GITHUB_ENV
      echo "IMAGE_TAG=${{ github.sha }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV

  # Now $IMAGE_TAG is available as a normal shell variable
  - name: Build Docker image
    run: docker build -t myapp:$IMAGE_TAG .

  # Step outputs (pass data to later steps in same job)
  - name: Get version
    id: version    # give the step an id to reference its output
    run: echo "version=$(cat package.json | jq -r .version)" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT

  - name: Print version
    run: echo "Version is ${{ steps.version.outputs.version }}"

content.text: Use concurrency to cancel stale runs. When you push 5 commits quickly, you don't want 5 CI runs to complete — only the latest matters. The concurrency block cancels any in-progress run for the same branch when a new one starts. This can cut your CI bill by 60% on fast-moving branches.

questions.question: Why use 'npm ci' instead of 'npm install' in CI?
options: npm ci is faster because it skips the audit check
npm ci installs from the lock file and fails if package.json and package-lock.json are out of sync — guaranteeing reproducible installs
npm install doesn't work in CI environments
npm ci automatically caches node_modules in the runner
questions.explanation: npm ci (clean install) always installs from package-lock.json, deletes node_modules first, and fails if the lockfile is out of date. npm install may update the lockfile or make different resolution decisions. In CI you want reproducible builds — same packages every run. npm ci guarantees this.

faq.q: How do I view workflow run results?
faq.a: Go to your repository on GitHub → Actions tab → click a workflow run → click a job → expand each step to see output and logs. You can also see the real-time stream while a workflow is running. Artifacts appear at the bottom of the workflow run summary page.

examples: Most GitHub repos enable 'Require status checks to pass before merging' — PRs can't be merged until the CI workflow passes, preventing broken code from reaching main
The concurrency block alone reduced CI costs by ~50% at many companies that had developers pushing frequently during active development
